artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a subset $A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, define its Fourier transform by
$$\widehat{A}(u)=\sum_{a\in A} e^{2\pi i a u/N},\qquad u\in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}.$$
Call $A$ $\varepsilon$-uniform if
$$\sum_{\substack{u\in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\\ u\neq 0}} |\widehat{A}(u)|^{4} \le \varepsilon N^{4}.$$
Decide whether the following statement is true: for every fixed integer $k\ge 1$ and every sufficiently small constant $c>0$, there exist a sequence of positive integers $N_1, N_2,\ldots$ and subsets $A_i\subseteq \mathbb{Z}/N_i\mathbb{Z}$ such that for all $i\ge 1$:
(i) $|A_i| \ge c\, N_i$;
(ii) $A_i$ is $\varepsilon_i$-uniform for some sequence $\varepsilon_i\to 0$;
(iii) the number of four-term arithmetic progressions contained in $A_i$ is at most $c^{k} N_i^{2}$.
artifact.category_tag: Additive combinatorics; Fourier-uniform sets and arithmetic progressions
artifact.status_search_result: The question (attributed to Ruzsa) remains open. The best-known construction, due to Gowers, gives Fourier-uniform sets of density α with 4-AP count at most α^{4+c}N² for a small c>0, which does not achieve arbitrary exponent k. Recent work (Sah–Sawhney–Zhao, 2023) reduces the problem for a natural class of constructions to an equivalent arithmetic Ramsey question and resolves the analogous problem for odd-length progressions k≥5, but Ruzsa's original question for 4-APs with arbitrary k is not resolved.

status_evidence.title: Uniform sets with few progressions via colorings (arXiv:2307.06914)
status_evidence.snippet: An affirmative answer to Ruzsa's question would follow from the existence of an N^{o(1)}-coloring of [N] without symmetrically colored 4-APs.
status_evidence.claim: Ruzsa's question on Fourier-uniform sets with few 4-APs is reduced to an arithmetic Ramsey question but remains open.

status_evidence.title: Fourier-uniform sets with few 4-term arithmetic progressions (Stanford talk)
status_evidence.snippet: Gowers constructed Fourier uniform sets with density α and 4-AP density at most α^{4+c}.
status_evidence.claim: Best known result toward Ruzsa's question is Gowers' α^{4+c} bound; arbitrary k still open.
